title: Self-Teaching Time Series to Speak
one_liner: A system learns to describe time series patterns by exploring captions on its own and using a built-in judge to decide which ones are right, without human-written examples.
lead: Explaining what happens in a time series (a sequence of measurements over time) matters for high-stakes decisions like medical monitoring or equipment maintenance. Normally you would show examples of correct explanations to a model so it learns by imitation. But finding experts to write those explanations is expensive and slow. This paper solves that by letting the model teach itself: it explores different explanations on its own, judges them by testing if they help solve a related task, and gets better through that self-feedback loop.

paras: Time series captioning means writing a clear sentence about what is happening in a stream of data points. A hospital monitor beeping steadily for 10 seconds needs explaining: normal, or tachycardia? A stock price series needs describing: rising trend, stable, or crash risk. When you train a model by traditional supervised learning (showing it thousands of correct answer pairs), you need real experts to write those captions. For complex patterns in medical, industrial, or financial data, experts are rare and their time is expensive.

A beginner might try labeling data themselves using rules (if value above 50, call it high; otherwise low). But real patterns are subtle: a small tremor at exactly the right frequency might signal equipment failure, while the same tremor elsewhere means noise. No simple rules capture that complexity. So people end up hiring specialists to annotate datasets, slowing research to a crawl.

callout.html: Instead of learning from human-labeled captions, the model explores captions itself and judges which ones are useful by testing them on a related task.

steps.text: The agent creates diverse candidate descriptions of the time series pattern.
A downstream task (like answering questions about the data) runs with each caption and measures success.
Higher task success means the caption was useful; lower success means it missed the real pattern.
The agent learns to generate captions more likely to score high on the reasoning task.
After many iterations, captions become accurate descriptions of what the data actually shows.

paras: The paper changes how captions are learned: instead of copying from human examples, the agent explores freely and learns from whether each caption works in practice. The object is the caption generation rule inside the agent.

hidden.name: caption utility
paras: The paper measures something invisible in captions: how useful they are for solving a reasoning task downstream. A caption like 'patient heart rate rising' gets a high score if a reasoning engine can use it to answer questions correctly (like 'is this tachycardia?'). A vague caption like 'something changed' scores low because it does not help.

The agent never sees raw labels (human-written captions). Instead it measures utility directly: run the reasoner with each candidate caption, see if downstream accuracy goes up or down. That signal teaches the agent which caption strategies work.

heat.caption: Darker means higher downstream task success; brighter means vague or misses the pattern.

reads.html: The system watches whether each caption helps a reasoning engine answer questions correctly, because a caption that accurately describes the real pattern will let the reasoner extract the information it needs to answer questions, while a vague or false caption blocks that information.
The outer loop computes a proxy reward by running a downstream reasoning task and measuring task success as the feedback signal.

paras: The inner loop (the caption agent) is free to explore: it generates different sentences without any constraints, trying diverse ideas. If there were no feedback, it would just generate noise. But the outer loop connects exploration to reality: it tests each caption by asking a reasoning system (a model that answers questions about the data) to work with that caption. If the reasoner solves tasks correctly using the caption, task accuracy rises. That accuracy rise is the reward signal.

The reasoner automatically judges whether the caption is truthful and useful. A caption that lies or misses the real pattern will cause the reasoner to fail or give wrong answers, because the reasoner's reasoning steps depend on accurate facts to produce correct outputs. A caption that hits the actual structure will help the reasoner succeed because the reasoner can trust the caption to be true and build its reasoning on solid ground. So the reasoner acts as a built-in teacher, without needing a human to write anything. Over time, the caption agent learns to generate only captions that pass this implicit test.

stages.s: Reasoning engine tests each caption on task
Task success or failure scores the caption

math.words: Agent loss equals negative reward times some penalty, where reward is how well the reasoner performs with the caption
symbols: the agent's training loss (what it tries to minimize)
downstream task success when using this caption
a constant controlling how much to discourage long or complex captions
length or entropy of the generated caption

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Caption A: 'rising trend'. Reasoner accuracy = 0.85 (good). Length = 2 words. Loss = -0.85 + 0.01 * 2 = -0.83.
Caption B: 'the value is increasing with some noise'. Reasoner accuracy = 0.84. Length = 8 words. Loss = -0.84 + 0.01 * 8 = -0.76.
Caption A has lower loss (closer to -1 is better for minimization). Agent learns that short, direct captions work best. After many iterations, only accurate short captions survive.

math.note: The negative reward steers the agent toward captions that help the downstream reasoner succeed, by nudging the numbers in the agent's weights in a direction that reduces loss.

charts.title: Supervised method (needs labels)
charts.note: Experts must annotate thousands of examples before training can begin.

charts.title: Self-teaching method (this paper)
charts.note: Agent learns to caption with only unlabeled time series; new domains need no new annotation work.

items.b: Reasoner feedback is weak or misleading.
items.html: If the downstream task is easy or has many solutions, the reasoner might give high scores to captions that are vague or even false. The agent learns bad habits from noisy feedback. Solution: use a challenging downstream task that truly requires accurate captions.

The agent might discover that repeating the same caption (e.g., 'no change detected') scores decently on many inputs, and stops exploring. Solution: add exploration penalties or diversity terms to encourage varied captions.

items.b: Reward signal is delayed or sparse.
items.html: If the reasoner is too slow or runs only occasionally, the agent gets sparse reward, making learning hard. Solution: run the reasoner frequently or use a fast approximation.

The agent stays curious and diverse because it explores many caption ideas, the reasoner provides honest feedback on whether captions help because task accuracy directly reflects caption quality, and the loop runs long enough for patterns to emerge because many iterations allow the agent to gradually refine its strategy based on consistent feedback signals.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small time series dataset (no caption labels needed). Implement the agent to generate short English descriptions, and a simple reasoner that answers yes-no questions about the data (e.g., 'is the trend rising?'). Run the inner loop to generate candidate captions, run the outer loop to score them using reasoner accuracy, and let the agent train for 100 iterations. Measure the caption quality by hand (does the learned caption describe the actual pattern?) because human judgment is the ground truth for whether a description is correct. Also measure by reasoner accuracy (does the reasoner perform better with the learned captions than with random noise?) because improved reasoner performance proves the captions carry real information about the time series.
demo.closing: The demo succeeds if learned captions are interpretable to humans, because that proves the agent discovered real patterns instead of gibberish, AND if they improve reasoner performance compared to random noise, because that proves the captions actually communicate the information the reasoner needs to solve tasks.
